questions.question_text: For the graph of $y > 2x-4$, what is the boundary line and which side is shaded?

options.why: Chose a solid line, but $>$ is a strict inequality so the boundary is dotted
The origin gives $0>2(0)-4=-4$ (true), so the origin side is shaded, which is above the line
Used a solid line for a strict $>$ and shaded the wrong side of the boundary

questions.solution_text: $y>2x-4$: strict sign gives a dotted line. Test $(0,0)$: $0>-4$ is true, so shade the side containing the origin, which is above the line.

questions.question_text: For the graph of $y \le -3x+1$, what is the boundary line and which side is shaded?

options.why: Chose a dotted line, but $\le$ includes the boundary so the line is solid
Test $(0,0)$: $0\le 1$ is true, so the origin side (below the line) is shaded, not above
Used a dotted line for an inclusive $\le$ and shaded the wrong side

questions.solution_text: $y\le -3x+1$: inclusive sign gives a solid line. Test $(0,0)$: $0\le 1$ is true, so shade below (the origin side).

questions.question_text: Rearranging $2x-5y > 20$ into the form $y=mx+c$ gives which inequality?

options.why: Forgot to reverse the inequality sign when dividing both sides by $-5$
Divided $20$ by $-5$ as $+4$ instead of $-4$
Kept the sign and mishandled the sign of the $x$ coefficient

questions.question_text: Rearranging $5x+2y \ge 10$ into the form $y=mx+c$ gives which inequality?

options.why: Reversed the sign, but dividing by the positive $2$ keeps the inequality unchanged
Dropped the negative sign on the $x$ coefficient after moving $5x$ across
Divided $10$ by $2$ but kept it negative
$0>3$ is a false statement, so the origin is not in the region
Substituting the origin gives $0$, not a positive value, so the test fails

options.text: No, because the boundary is solid
options.why: The line style does not decide membership; substitution does, and $0>3$ is false

questions.solution_text: $4(0)-0=0$, and $0>3$ is false, so $(0,0)$ does not satisfy the inequality.

questions.question_text: Which point lies in the region defined by $x+2y \le 6$?

options.why: $4+2(3)=10$, and $10\le 6$ is false, so this point is outside
$6+2(1)=8$, and $8\le 6$ is false, so this point is outside
$0+2(4)=8$, and $8\le 6$ is false, so this point is outside

questions.solution_text: $(2,1)$: $2+2(1)=4$, and $4\le 6$ is true, so $(2,1)$ lies in the region.

questions.question_text: For the graph of $x < -1$, what is the boundary and which side is shaded?

options.text: Dotted vertical line $x=-1$; shade to the left
Solid vertical line $x=-1$; shade to the left
options.why: $<$ is strict, so the vertical boundary is dotted, not solid

options.text: Dotted vertical line $x=-1$; shade to the right
options.why: $x<-1$ means smaller $x$-values, which lie to the left of the line
$x<-1$ is a condition on $x$, so the boundary is vertical, not horizontal

questions.solution_text: $x<-1$ has a vertical dotted boundary $x=-1$; smaller $x$-values lie to the left, so shade left.

questions.question_text: Using the test point $(0,0)$ for $y < x+1$, which region is shaded?

options.text: The side containing $(0,0)$, below the line
The side not containing $(0,0)$, above the line
options.why: $0<0+1$ is true, so the origin IS in the region and its side is shaded
A strict inequality shades a half-plane, not just the line
Only the half-plane on the origin's side is shaded, not the entire plane

questions.solution_text: Test $(0,0)$: $0<0+1=1$ is true, so shade the half-plane containing the origin (below the line).
